entries.title: ‘Bold, brilliant, thrilling’: leading authors on the novels every school should teach
entries.summary: A new term, a new PM … time for a new English curriculum? We ask writers from Ben Okri to Samantha Harvey to pick books that will inspire a lifelong love of readingFor the first time ever, we have a British prime minister who studied for an English degree. entries.content:
For the first time ever, we have a British prime minister who studied for an English degree. Not all of his 58 predecessors went to university, but those who did favoured subjects such as history and classics and, more recently, philosophy, politics and economics. Yet reading fiction is a fantastic preparation for life, for understanding people and the times through which we live. Novels encourage empathy, they help you to stand in other people’s shoes, to navigate complicated, sometimes conflicting emotions, they entertain and bring joy. The creative industries contribute some £145.8bn each year to the UK economy; it is our soft superpower.

In other words, books matter. Reading matters.

However, there has been a marked decline over recent years in the numbers of children reading for pleasure. It’s why the National Literacy Trust designated 2026 the National Year of Reading. Already there has been a shift from a 20-year low in 2025 of 32.7% of eight-to-18-year-olds saying they enjoy reading in their free time up to 36.1%. It’s a start.

We are also in a long-overdue moment of curriculum renewal for GCSE English, so when better to ask if what’s studied in school helps young people fall in love with reading – or possibly puts them off for life?

Since GCSEs were first introduced in 1986, we’ve seen the establishment of four main examination boards in England and Wales and surprising unanimity in the choice of books most schools choose to teach. In 2025, the educational charity End Sexism in Schools released a report – Manopolies – revealing that 76% of students study An Inspector Calls by JB Priestley for their modern text from a possible 21 modern texts (a play, wonderful as it is, that’s been on one board’s set text list for 39 years). Then a whopping 93% of students study either A Christmas Carol by Charles Dickens or The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde by Robert Louis Stevenson for their 19th-century novel from nine possible texts (including Charlotte Brontë, Mary Shelley and Jane Austen). Only 5% of students in England and Wales study a female-authored text at GCSE.

It’s true that there are diverse modern works by inspirational women on the lists of the four exam boards – Kit de Waal, Tanika Gupta, Jeanette Winterson, Malorie Blackman are all offered. The problem is that schools are disincentivised to change the texts they teach as this would involve costs and additional work. And no exam board wants to be the one to remove popular texts because that would bring commercial disadvantage and developmental costs. This is why it’s essential the Department for Education, as part of this review, mandates the regular changing of set-text lists and stipulates that students study works that reflect the gender balance and diversity of our society. Schools can’t do it on their own.

Here, to get the conversation started, are suggestions of texts to inspire a passion for fiction in young readers. And, from me, a plea for the government to support teachers who want to better reflect the gender balance and diversity of their classrooms.

This is the way to encourage a lifelong love of reading.

Kate Mosse

Nussaibah Younis

The Trees by Percival Everett

Wouldn’t it be refreshing to see a blisteringly funny novel on the syllabus? The Trees is a daring satire on racism, generational guilt and cultural complicity, inspired by the lynching of Emmett Till. Genre-bending and gloriously inventive, it finds morbid delight in the absurdities of American racial violence without ever trivialising its victims. With characters such as Dr Reverend Fondle, Junior Junior and Hot Mama Yeller, Everett exposes the grotesque stupidity of white supremacy through comedy that is as vicious as it is exhilarating. What better way to show teenagers that literature can be genuinely enjoyable, even laugh-out-loud funny, while remaining intellectually and morally serious.

Frank Cottrell-Boyce

Stories of Your Life and Others by Ted Chiang

A great short story hits you like a left hook or an unexpected kiss – coming out of nowhere and leaving you gasping, what just happened? Which is the perfect state for learning, of course. Short stories work really well in the classroom because reading is best when it’s shared. I would, therefore, strongly suggest Ted Chiang’s astonishing science fiction collection Stories of Your Life and Others. Each story takes on a big idea – language, love, intelligence, the collateral damage to real estate that angels might cause when intervening in human affairs, that sort of thing. They go off in your head like bombs. The most famous is the title story, which was made into the movie Arrival. Teenagers love ideas. They’re about to go into a world that their grownups are viewing as some kind of sci-fi nightmare. Here’s a bold, brilliant, thrilling set of thought experiments about how it could be OK after all. It’s a science fiction collection that opens with a story set in Old Testament Babylon. What else do you need to know?

Patrice Lawrence

Random by Debbie Tucker Green

I recommend this play. For a Black working-class London family, it’s a normal weekday – until the teenage son is senselessly stabbed and killed.

The work is performed by one actor, from the point of view of the sister. The dialogue is funny, tenderly painting the warm family relationships until that one moment destroys everything. Then follows grief, fury, helplessness and despair.

Random is gripping and short. It’s a springboard for many different conversations, from topics such as the impact of race in the criminal justice system and the representation of working-class families, to the benefits and challenges of performing such an emotional piece in a stripped-back set.

David Mitchell

The Rest of Us Just Live Here by Patrick Ness

This wise, chaotic, gentle, painful, funny, superb novel follows five teens trying to navigate the most difficult year of their lives, while the town’s cool indie kids are battling Stranger Things-sized perils in vignettes at the start of each chapter. It contains some of the truest (and helpful) lines about social anxiety I’ve ever read. For reluctant readers, The Rest of Us Just Live Here proves that great fiction is as compelling as a great video game; and unlike social media, it leaves you feeling nourished, smarter, and not wanting back the time you just spent on it. I was asked to provide one title only, but hey: class, now turn to that blast of medieval Tarantino, The Pardoner’s Tale. Chaucer, Patrick Ness and the language we’re using right now cohabit the same glorious entangled continuum. Compare and contrast Henry IV Part 2 Act 3 Scene 1, “Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown” with the lyrics to Stormzy’s song Crown. Art is made of art. It speaks across centuries. Now it’s your turn.

Hollie McNish

Wild Geese by Mary Oliver

After spending many evenings this spring testing my daughter on her GCSE English Literature quotes, I felt ready to vomit. Three set texts: Lord of the Flies, Macbeth and The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde. Shared themes of blood, death, murder, violence, the evil of boys and men. Then, if you’re tired of revising prose, a little war poetry for a breather. Lovely. More death.

In those two exam years, my daughter studied not one female prose writer, not one writer of colour, only four female characters in the entire trio of set texts (if you count Macbeth’s witches as individual characters, which is debatable, oh and a female pig, according to one teacher). Nearly 30 years ago, my experience was almost exactly the same.

What a way to teach a love of literature; what a way to normalise only reading books by men about men, and only if violence is centre stage of the men’s worlds. English literature is an amazing opportunity to nurture a joy of reading, to open minds to other cultures and worlds and wonders. So why is every single text soaked in bloodshed? If I were to pick a text for young people to study, I’d suggest anything but more violence. Something loving, anything funny; just one book teenagers could smile at, laugh with even. Perhaps Ocean Vuong’s The Emperor of Gladness, a gorgeous story between a young man and an elderly woman. Or maybe on the poetry curriculum, Wild Geese by Mary Oliver. Something that has helped people the world over to feel more joy.

Ben Okri

African Stories edited by Ben Okri

One of the weaknesses of the literary education of this country is that students are not exposed early in life to the valuable literatures of non-European people, particularly Africans.

This Everyman African Stories anthology brings together 36 classical African stories written in, or translated into, English. It tracks nearly 100 years and observes every aspect of life, from the domestic to the political, from the romantic to the existential.

An average Briton could go through a whole lifetime of wide reading without ever reading any classic African text. These stories would not only provide entertaining and enlightening reading, they could serve as a gateway to discovering the rich literature of a much-overlooked continent.

Kamila Shamsie

Small Things Like These by Claire Keegan

If you look at the most often assigned GCSE texts, the common denominator is a word count under 30,000. That factor knocks a great many wonderful books off the list, but it does also allow space for the brilliance of Claire Keegan. I’d choose Small Things Like These, a novel of remarkable depth within its brevity. “How does she do it?” is a question for any reader of the book – but there are plenty of other questions in it for students. The novel’s story within a story, its use of memory, the character of Bill Furlong, the internal and external landscapes, and the history of the Magdalene laundries are all rich ground for thought and discussion. No harm either in letting young readers recognise that what appears small and quiet is actually taut and fierce.

Andrew McMillan

100 Queer Poems edited by Mary Jean Chan and Andrew McMillan

There has never been a more important time to ensure that our school libraries and our class curricula contain plenty of books by, about and for LGBTQ+ people. When Mary Jean Chan and I were co-editing 100 Queer Poems, it felt like making something that I needed to read when I was in secondary school. Anthologies are great to study because they allow for the necessity of not liking something. With 100 poets published by more than 45 different presses, a reader won’t enjoy all the different styles and schools of poetry on offer, but they might find some that strike a spark of recognition. There might be one poem that helps a student in developing their own individual language for articulating who they are, and who they might become, in the world.

Kit de Waal

Fallout by Eleanor Anstruther

Set in 1982, Fallout is a fictionalised account of the Greenham Common protest as seen through the eyes of a rebellious 15-year-old girl. Non-preachy, funny and sharp, it’s about family secrets, female empowerment and an important time in British history that we are in danger of forgetting.

I’d also suggest Every Man for Himself by Beryl Bainbridge, which is as much about class as it is about the sinking of the Titanic. It’s a sort of whodunnit seen through the eyes of a young man who falls in love with an unobtainable young woman shortly before disaster strikes. It mixes fact with fiction, and the way it’s structured means you have to read it right to the end.

Geoff Dyer

Voyage in the Dark by Jean Rhys

Two things are of the utmost importance. To adhere to quality as the criterion of, well, of the utmost importance! And to give a sense of the evolving tradition of literature, rather than catering to a preference for the contemporary. The problem is that some things formerly deemed of high quality – crucial components of that tradition – now seem of dubious quality.

The good news is that the reputations of plenty of female writers from the interwar period continue to soar. And many of the themes and concerns that preoccupy us now were being addressed by these writers almost a century ago. No one exemplifies this more than Jean Rhys, a writer of genius whose four novels, from 1928 and into the 1930s, were so far ahead of their time that they were doomed, like her heroines, to failure and obscurity. They also have the appealing virtue of extreme brevity, weighing in at about 150 pages apiece.

If obliged to select just one of these, I would go for the third, Voyage in the Dark (1934), her devastating and funny account of 18-year-old Anna, who comes from the West Indies and finds herself alone and helpless in London. The perfect introduction to that sought after but mysterious ideal of a writer’s “voice”, it will leave new readers wanting to venture further into Rhys’s strangely defamiliarised world. Which means, in turn, that they will be drawn to her final masterpiece, Wide Sargasso Sea, and from there, inevitably, to Brontë’s Jane Eyre.

Samantha Harvey

Moon Tiger by Penelope Lively

Moon Tiger is a life story and a love story, the story of a woman called Claudia who, we learn on page one, is on her deathbed, ransacking her memories in order to give an account of herself. “Shake the tube and see what comes out,” she says. “Chronology irritates me. There is no chronology inside my head.” The story she tells is seductive, searching, confronting and compressed; scenes are played and differently replayed, truth is questioned, the idea of selfhood is dismantled.

Although it’s the retrospection of an older woman, there’s something in this exploded, chaotic rendition of self that would have struck me hard in my teens – the self as a beautiful, dangerous, vulnerable mess. It’s about the harm we do and suffer, and about the possibility of happiness. The whole novel is hot to the touch. It pushes at what a novel can do. It’s experimental in the best, most necessary of ways and a perfect study of how narrative works. Nearly 40 years on, the writing is still fresh, gorgeous and daring. And, admittedly, quite sexy. English teachers up and down the country might be less enthusiastic about it being on the curriculum than I am.

Benjamin Myers

Address Unknown by Kathrine Kressmann Taylor

This epistolary novel is told via a series of letters between two business partners from 1932 to 1934 – Max is an art gallerist in the US while Martin has returned to their fatherland, where he is immediately energised by a bold new leader. But soon the hatred seeps in, and Martin asks his friend to cease communication lest he himself be mistakenly identified as a collaborator. Little more need be said about the plot, other than that it is a one-sitting/one‑lesson/one-hour read that challenges notions of friendship, loyalty, antisemitism and the sheer insidiousness of totalitarian regimes. Trump, Farage, Musk, Putin – all are reflected in Kressmann Taylor’s powerfully concise prose, perfectly constructed for the permanently distracted. Pair with Fred Uhlman’s equally economical 1932-set novel Reunion for a “compare and contrast” discussion -starter.

Raymond Antrobus

Glyph by Ali Smith

Few contemporary novels manage to be this urgent and playful at once, which is exactly why it belongs in a classroom: it proves seriousness and playfulness aren’t opposites. At its centre are two estranged sisters, Petra and Patricia, grieving their mother and reckoning with childhood trauma. Smith threads their story through three wars: a horse blinded in the first world war; a flattened body found in the second; and the present-day war in Gaza. The novel asks what it means to watch history repeat itself while insisting it won’t. A ghost horse, conjured by the sisters as children, returns decades later to disturb the present, blurring memory, myth and reality in ways that reward close, repeated reading. Throughout, Smith’s inventive wordplay, puns, homophones – and the title, which mirrors its companion novel Gliff – make language itself a subject, not just a vehicle. Students would leave Glyph asking what stories are for, and whether imagination is escapism or the most soulful technology we have for facing a broken, divided society.

entries.title: The best recent poetry – review roundup
entries.summary: Fetch by Colin Bramwell; Girling by Eve Esfandiari-Denney; The Dead One, The Unconscious One, Thundering in Your Ear, Thriving Slumber by Jay Gao; Belling the Leopard by Clementine Ewokolo Burnley; The Matter by Padraig ReganFetch by Colin Bramwell (And Other Stories, £14.99)Bramwell’s translation of Fernando Pessoa’s work into Scots won him considerable recognition: it took the Oxford Weidenfeld
entries.content:
Fetch by Colin Bramwell (And Other Stories, £14.99)

Bramwell’s translation of Fernando Pessoa’s work into Scots won him considerable recognition: it took the Oxford Weidenfeld Translation prize and the Highland Book Prize. Between source and target language, there is always a gap; the translator endeavours within that gap to identify meaning and intention, and that is the difficult work of translation. Fetch, Bramwell’s own debut collection, lyrically thematises this gap in the poet-human’s condition: “I’m an instrument for something else / a digital piano that if you opened it up / you wouldn’t understand the wiring.” Fetch (in Celtic folklore, a doppelganger) is by turns solemnly tender, comically worldly, literarily devout. Here you’ll find deep engagement with Russian poets such as Osip Mandelstam and Anna Akhmatova, poems that fuse Scots and English, alongside filial memories and premonitions of fatherhood. “Death is certain, but back then I was too young for that shit.” For a debut, Bramwell’s poetics convey an uncanny sense of wisdom, patience and, eventually, peace.

Girling by Eve Esfandiari-Denney (Fitzcarraldo, £12.99)

Before theme and subject, there is the pure, iridescent beauty of Esfandiari-Denney’s sentences; a singular voice that is alluring and sensuous, pleasurable to follow to whichever subject the poet chooses. The subjects are girlhood-cum-womanhood, the line between debilitating illness and delusional wellness (“thank god / you invested / in lion’s mane”), the flickering concept of free will for a species so programmed by genes: “I have wondered to what extent my cancer diagnosis is my mother’s, or my grandmother’s cell mutation, before my own … I look up from a cigarette mid-sentence…” The collection hybridises recognisable prose forms: the essay, the diary, the text message, the anecdote. These are interspliced with short-lined lyric poems that startle because of the bubbly voice from which they come: “I hope it’s ok to die. I can / become something / like actualised metaphor.” The magic of this collection is that it is never highfalutin, finding a way to make an ending like “DJ are you listening did you read to the end will you blow my voice a kiss” powerfully funny and moving.

The Dead One, The Unconscious One, Thundering in Your Ear, Thriving Slumber by Jay Gao (Carcanet, £12.99)

“This is how the buried live. Poetry”. The title of this collection alone will illuminate what kind of poet Gao is: insistent, sprawling, and conceptually daring. The poems in this collection are not spoken by a tree, but rather embody a tree’s form, each line like a budding leaf, simultaneously discreet, and genetically preordained by the bark from which it sprouts: “Mustering diction in the interest of the non-human”; “On the horizon, a filthy war dog shakes her remaindered vernal atoms free”; or, one of my favourite lines, “You wanted the intimacy of two words who shared a sound to unsecure that wild”. Every couple of pages there are “splinters”, single words with ultra-long dashes that could grammatically and sonically replace a word in the preceding line: “A splinter of duration lodged inside times’ ruche, awaiting salvage …” is followed by a page-long em-dash before the word “selvedge”. Gao joins the ranks of poets such as CD Wright and Lyn Hejinian: not for the faint of heart, but an endless well of brilliance and deep feeling if one can undergo their clause-by-clause compressive inventions.

Belling the Leopard by Clementine Ewokolo Burnley (Bloodaxe, £14)

There’s an imaginative heaviness to Belling the Leopard, so composed of the proper names of people, places and things that each poem feels like a constructed miniature: “Liberated Africans, Jamaicans, and English / missionaries lived side by side in eight / corrugated iron shelters shipped / from Clarence.” The forced migrations and enslavement of colonialism create a latticework of place across the collection, which is Burnley’s primary structuring principle. Between the Caribbean, western Africa and western Europe, Burnley describes the intimate violence and domestic and cultural fallout of their comingling histories: “All the flights from Africa used to transit through a European capital city. Ethiopian Airlines no longer touches down in the nine hours it takes to fly from Turtle Island to Togo. Sometimes the border agencies use commercial flights for deportations.” At times, this debut collection feels overwritten, certain narratives more like onslaughts of information and impression with little effect. It is at its best when memory and lyric fuse, where the line between recounting and reshaping blurs: “We rub each other raw in the same spots / and if you’re starting to lose / arguments, I notice I no longer need to win.” There’s much to admire here.

The Matter by Padraig Regan (Carcanet, £12.99)

Regan’s sophomore collection echoes the structure of their first: lyric poem sequences with a long(ish) essay splitting up the sections. Here, they intensify their engagements with the material world, “chiefly animals, minerals and vegetables”. Lines from the poem A Venus Flower Basket sum up the stylistic changes Regan has made, from parsed syntactical lines to more high-octane fragmentations: “Drowned Arachne! / except: what it spins / it is. & who wouldn’t / want to wear their bones / on the outside / if they could sparkle”. Elsewhere, the poet addresses Gogotte, a naturally occurring “concretion of very fine, very pure sands”, primarily found in France. Gogotte has a way of looking like finely sculpted ceramic work, allowing the poet to drift from the geological to musings on the body’s evanescence, gay saunas, and language itself: “I am a poet, Gogotte: I spend my life trying to come up with verbal structures commensurate with the unstructurable mess of being-in-the world.” Though the collection can feel unevenly motley in some aspects, Regan has a knack for startling detail and lush description, as in the poem A Belemnite: “An off white seam runs jagged / down its length / like an injury; // its surface is a register / of glances & impacts / against whose grain I read the // long, posthumous biography”. This voice can be spellbinding.

entries.title: The Golden Hours by Louisa Young review – this continuation of the Cazalet Chronicles is a total delight
entries.summary: Elizabeth Jane Howard’s niece has picked up the thread of her much-loved family saga series, taking the story into the 1960sElizabeth Jane Howard’s beloved family saga the Cazalet Chronicles spans three decades in the life of the upper-middle-class Cazalet family. entries.content:
Elizabeth Jane Howard’s beloved family saga the Cazalet Chronicles spans three decades in the life of the upper-middle-class Cazalet family. The first four books, written in the 1990s, run from a bucolic prewar 1937 to a bruising 1947, while the fifth, 2013’s All Change, skips ahead, sitting lonely in 1956. The books are exquisite doll’s houses of feeling and object: both period detail and eternal emotion are rendered precisely and vigorously in Howard’s lovely prose. “Panoramic, expansive, intriguing as social history and generous in their storytelling,” Hilary Mantel wrote in the Guardian. The enormous cast of characters – four late-Victorian siblings, their parents, their children and partners and ex-partners and servants and friends and lovers and enemies and cars and houses – sprawl deliciously over the years. The family fortunes rise and fall. Marriages fail; deaths occur; babies are born; people fall in love. Things change; things stay the same.

Written a decade after the death of the original author, The Golden Hours by Louisa Young adds a sixth to this quintet. As with all Cazalet novels, to describe the plot would be impossible: it is simply that many people, whom we have come to love over the course of the previous novels, live their lives, now in the early 1960s.

Polly, first encountered as a serious and beautiful child almost 30 years earlier, is now the chatelaine of a falling-down country house. This house has replaced the original Home Place as the centre of family life: it’s Christmas, and the siblings gather at Polly’s home. The next generation take up much of the narrative, picking up the loose threads that Howard set down: what will Louise do with her life? Can Clary and Zoe and Rupert and Archie really all live together in one house? And what, for the love of God, is going to happen to Neville?

There is little more controversial, to the serious reader, than a so-called “continuation novel”: a sequel written by somebody else, with little or no input from the original creator (who is mostly, in such cases, beyond the grave). Can it be done? Should it be done? Can creations continue to live without their creators? Mortality need not present a challenge to those readers who wish for more (or publishers who wish for more of their money). Eoin Colfer was given the keys to the Hitchhiker’s Guide; Sophie Hannah became Poirot’s posthumous puppeteer. Sebastian Faulks, an overachiever, has been both Bond and Jeeves. Young has two significant advantages: first, this is her 16th book; second, Howard was Young’s own personal beloved “Aunt Jane”. There is something pleasing about a family saga being continued by the author’s own family – but the stakes are, perhaps, even higher.

Happily, however, Young’s gamble has paid off: The Golden Hours is a total delight. It is not the flawless The Light Years, but it is not remotely out of place in the series. It takes a couple of chapters to settle fully into Howard’s voice, but achieves a startling mimicry that drew even this sceptical reader along for the ride. Young tackles several of the trickier problems posed by Howard – Neville again! – without shying away from her frank clarity into the human mind. If the dialogue is occasionally a little more contrived than Howard’s, and a few of the forays into big-picture thinking verge on the glib (“the problem wasn’t what you were, it was how people treated you for what you were”), then these things can be forgiven for the sheer pleasure of coming home.

And if things are different, well, then things are different. Any series written over 23 years will trace not just the ways the characters change, but the ways the writer changed in the writing. There is, perhaps, a greater gulf between The Light Years and Howard’s final novel All Change than between All Change and The Golden Hours; or even between The Light Years and The Golden Hours.

Writers change, as indeed people change; and yet humanity stays the same. And this is, in many ways, the great unifying theme of this book and the series as a whole. “Are things exactly the same, or mortally different?” muses one-time chauffeur Tonbridge. Another character quotes the Oracle at Delphi: “Know Thyself on one end; Things Change on the other …”

And this, perhaps, is the secret to writing a great continuation – or, in fact, the secret to writing anything. Things change; know thyself. Young understands both. A new generation takes up the mantle of the next generation of Cazalets: with a seventh and eighth volume promised, long may it continue.

entries.title: Kevin Powers: ‘I was ready to abandon Infinite Jest a thousand times’
entries.summary: The American author on falling in love with The Great Gatsby, being inspired by Dylan Thomas – and the memoir of a canoe trip in Texas he comes back toMy earliest reading memoryThe deaths of Old Dan and Little Ann in Wilson Rawls’s Where the Red Fern Grows were etched into my being as a first grader in Chesterfield County, Virginia.My favourite book growing upStephen King’s The Stand. I completely
entries.content:
My earliest reading memory

The deaths of Old Dan and Little Ann in Wilson Rawls’s Where the Red Fern Grows were etched into my being as a first grader in Chesterfield County, Virginia.

My favourite book growing up

Stephen King’s The Stand. I completely lost myself in the story. I don’t think I realised at the time what a rare gift it is to have that experience.

The book that changed me as a teenager

When I was 12 or 13, I wandered into the modest poetry section of our local used bookstore and was drawn to the cover art of Dylan Thomas’s Collected Poems. I flipped it open and read, “Now as I was young and easy under the apple boughs …” I won’t pretend I was a sophisticated reader of poetry at the time, but the music was undeniable. I wrote my first attempt at poetry that night and knew from that moment I would chase that music for the rest of my life.

The writer who changed my mind

I read GK Chesterton’s Orthodoxy when I was in my early 20s. His framing of tradition as democracy extended to the dead was something I’d never considered, and frankly, found quite persuasive. My politics didn’t change, but I discovered how essential it is to have your ideas challenged, and how foolish it is to believe your opinions are correct simply because you are the one who holds them.

The book that made me want to be a writer

F Scott Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby, at school, when I was 15 or 16. I fell so deeply in love with the book that, and this is somewhat embarrassing to admit, I would type out sentences from it on my family’s old desktop computer just to see what it felt like.

The book or author I came back to

I had a friend in graduate school who was such an evangelist for David Foster Wallace’s Infinite Jest that he would give me pep talks each of the thousand times I was ready to abandon it. When I finally got to Don Gately’s portion of the narrative, the book completely opened up to me, and I now deeply admire it.

The book I reread

I moved to Texas in my 20s and was recommended John Graves’s Goodbye to a River, a memoir of a final canoe trip down the Brazos River before it was meant to be dammed up. The writing is exquisite. For me it’s the platonic ideal of a book as the record of a mind at work. I’ve reread it every year or two ever since.

The book I could never read again

Thomas Wolfe’s Look Homeward, Angel was another transformative work I read as a teenager. I’m afraid I wouldn’t like it if I read it again, and I don’t want to take that joy away from my 16-year-old self.

The book I discovered later in life

I read Pär Lagerkvist’s Barabbas only a few years ago, and it has become a touchstone for clarity in my own writing. There are scenes that are among the most deeply moving yet plainly told as anything I’ve ever read.

The book I am currently reading

I just finished Foster by Claire Keegan and immediately ordered everything she’s ever published.

My comfort read

If I’m honest, I think I read to be made uncomfortable.

entries.title: Gloria Steinem, groundbreaking feminist campaigner, dies aged 92
entries.summary: Prolific author campaigned against domestic violence, female genital mutilation, pornography and the Vietnam and Gulf wars‘We badly need to raise our boys more like our girls’: Gloria Steinem – a life in quotesHillary Clinton leads tributes to Gloria Steinem: ‘Her activism was rooted in optimism’Gloria Steinem, the American feminist and journalist whose activism helped push through greater rights
entries.content:
Gloria Steinem, the American feminist and journalist whose activism helped push through greater rights for women around the world has died, aged 92.

Steinem “passed away peacefully at her home in New York City, surrounded by some of the many who loved her”, a statement shared to her Instagram page said.

“Gloria’s near-century on earth were years well-lived, and she continued working for equality until the very end,” the post added. “Gloria’s greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard. Her words, actions, and example gave people permission to be their truest selves.”

Steinem brought a feminist perspective into the mainstream through rigorous journalism, public speaking and activism. The author of nine books, she campaigned against domestic violence, female genital mutilation, the pornography industry and the Vietnam and Gulf wars. She also worked in support of causes including Black Lives Matter, the reunification of Korea, female reproductive rights, LGBTQ+ rights and the Times Up movement. In 1984, she was arrested while protesting against apartheid outside the South African embassy in Washington DC.

Outside Steinem’s elegant, classic townhouse in Manhattan’s Upper East Side neighbourhood on Thursday morning, passersby left tributes.

Debbie Goldberg, who said she lived close by, placed a bunch of red flowers next to the steps up to the front door.

“I’ve never done that before. But she deserved it,” she said, describing Steinem as one of the most influential people for women’s rights and human rights in history.

“She’s a hero to all women whether they know it or not,” she said.

Goldberg said that she saw Steinem speak in Washington DC “around 30 years ago”, and then bumped into her as they were both heading into a cinema a few blocks away to see the Barbie movie in 2023. Goldberg said had been planning to watch Steinem speak in a few weeks’ time at a YMCA close by. “She’s always been an idol of mine,” Goldberg added.

Others left a bouquet of roses mixed with a variety of blooms in pink and white, and a large seashell filled with gems and other trinkets.

Born in Ohio in 1934, Steinem grew up in a trailer home. Her mother’s mental illness left her struggling to hold on to work and in and out of sanatoriums. When she was 10, her parents separated and, while growing up in a rundown home in Toledo with her mother, Steinem began to notice the hostility her mother endured as a working woman.

After graduating from a women’s liberal arts college in 1956, Steinem travelled to India for two years, where she worked as a legal clerk in the country’s supreme court. Returning to the US, she worked as the director of the Independent Research Service, a CIA front that recruited American students to disrupt the Soviet-controlled World Youth Festivals in Vienna and Helsinki. Steinem later revealed she had always known who was bankrolling the operation: “If I had a choice I would do it again.”

In 1962, she received her first “serious assignment” in journalism from the Esquire magazine editor, Clay Felker. Her feature on contraception, The Moral Disarmament of Betty Coed, detailed how women were forced to choose between careers and family. The following year, Steinem went undercover as a Playboy Bunny for 11 days, to write her infamous, two-part exposé of how the glamour models were treated while working in Hugh Hefner’s Playboy Club. Forced into tight costumes and high heels, Steinem lost 10lb – half of them in a single night – during her stint; her manager celebrated by making her costume two inches tighter. Following the article, she was unable to get work because “because I had now become a Bunny – and it didn’t matter why”.

In 1968, Felker hired her to work at New York magazine, in which she would coin the term “reproductive freedom” for an article about an abortion “speakout” in Greenwich Village. Having had an abortion in London when was 22, she later described feeling a “big click” while at the protest and said the day marked the start of her life as an “active feminist”.

“I think the person who said: ‘Honey, if men could get pregnant, abortion would be a sacrament’ was right,” she told the Observer in 2011. “Speaking for myself, I knew it was the first time I had taken responsibility for my own life. I wasn’t going to let things happen to me. I was going to direct my life, and therefore it felt positive.”

She also credited black feminists including Florynce Kennedy, Evelyn Cunningham, Shirley Chisholm and Fannie Lou Hamer for teaching her the importance of activism. “It was like finding a family,” she said of that time. “As wildly different as we may be, and we certainly were, women share hopes and a certain vision of the world, and a certain shit detector.”

This also began Steinem’s career as a provocative journalist, penning articles including If Men Could Menstruate, which ran in Ms, a magazine co-founded by Steinem and Dorothy Pitman Hughes in 1971. The first issue featured Wonder Woman on the cover; the superhero had recently given up her powers to stay with her male love interest, and the essay argued that DC Comics should restore her powers and return the character to her feminist roots. Steinem also wrote articles such as What It Would Be Like If Women Win in Time, and After Black Power, Women’s Liberation, the 1969 New York magazine article that would make her name as a feminist leader.

Terrified of public speaking and conflict, but media savvy, Steinem used the platform she gained as a white, educated woman to speak out for those traditionally ignored – black people, ethnic minorities and the working class. Sex and race were always intertwined, she argued in 1971, “because they are easy, and visible differences have been the primary ways of organising human beings into superior and inferior groups and into the cheap labour on which this system still depends.” In 2017, she said: “It doesn’t surprise me that the most virulent anti-abortion measures are coming from Alabama and other southern states because racism and sexism are always intertwined. You can’t perpetuate racism without controlling women and reproduction.”

Steinem was also a polarising figure. Some feminists felt her position as a public leader in the movement had been decided not by merit but by the media, which chose her for being young, white and attractive; in her 2015 book My Life on the Road, she wrote that the “idea that whatever I had accomplished was all about looks would remain a biased and hurtful accusation even into my old age”.

She was roundly criticised for decades for a 1998 opinion piece for the New York Times, in which she supported President Bill Clinton in the face of sexual harassment allegations. “He is not guilty of sexual harassment,” she wrote, only “a gross, dumb, and reckless pass at a supporter during a low point in her life”. In 2017, she said: “We have to believe women. I wouldn’t write the same thing now because there’s probably more known about other women now.” She was also regarded as hostile to transgender rights because of a piece she wrote in 1977, a position she clarified in 2013: “I believe that transgender people, including those who have transitioned, are living out real, authentic lives. Those lives should be celebrated, not questioned.”

In 1986, Steinem was diagnosed with breast cancer, then in 1994 the chronic pain condition trigeminal neuralgia. After years of dismissing marriage, she married the environmental activist David Bale in 2000, and remained close with her stepson, the actor Christian Bale, after his father’s death in 2003.

Having supported Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign, Steinem was a prominent critic of Donald Trump, co-chairing and speaking at the Women’s March on Washington, a mass protest held the day after the Trump’s inauguration in January 2017. “The only good news of Trump is that the galvanising of activism is like nothing I have ever seen in my life,” she told the Guardian that year. “A thousand times more even than the Vietnam war, and how important that was – or of any other thing I’ve ever seen.”

In 2011, she told the Observer: “I hope to live to 100. There is so much to do.”

Anna Betts contributed reporting from New York

entries.content:
Irvine Welsh, author

I’ve been enjoying Contrapposto by Dave Eggers. The premise that love and art are the only things that make life worthwhile pulses beautifully through this novel and its two protagonists, spanning decades of their obsession with both, and each other. The tragedy is they are not sufficient alone for a relationship to survive to the exclusion of everything else (namely capitalism, which always has a place at the table), but they remain essential and enduring. Nowhere is this better evoked than here. Think John Williams’s Stoner but with art instead of literature and stuffed with more memorable characters.

In Raveheart, Graeme Armstrong confronts the twin promises of utopia and madness in a time before the internet’s colonisation of the mind, when people still dared to dream and lived to party. This book made me want to call some heads, rent a farmhouse, get a sound system and neck several pills. In fact, I might just do that.

Finally, another one for creatures of the night in all their disparate glory. Overnight by Dan Richards is more than a tribute to the people (and other critters) who operate in the hours of darkness to ensure we have everything we need – it’s a discourse on the very nature of night-time itself, and its essential relationship to our humanity. This is a beautifully written work of startling brilliance, astonishing the reader page after page.

Can Nothing Save Us? by Irvine Welsh is published by Jonathan Cape (£20). To support the Guardian, buy a copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

Jean, Guardian reader

I am reading The Shampoo Effect by Jenny Jackson. My only regret is not saving this book until my late summer beach vacation, because this book is best read with sand betwixt your toes. The story follows a group of lifelong friends in their thirties in their Massachusetts home town as they navigate marriage, parenthood, and careers. A newcomer from New York City arrives to work on what she hopes will be her big break as a writer and becomes irrevocably interwoven in the group’s complicated dynamics. It’s funny, sharp, and has me wondering as a child-free woman if many parents are self-medicating with weed on a regular basis to get through the day.

Janice Hallett, author

I’ve been diving deep into true crime lately. London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe is a book that examines so much more than its central crime story: that of a young man whose big dreams and relentless drive took him in a deadly direction. Keefe elevates the tragedy by placing it in the context of our capital’s criminal history. I’ve also revisited Carol Ann Lee’s exceptionally researched and presented The Murders at White House Farm.

For someone fascinated by criminal psychology and the legal system, this book is without a doubt a core text on the Jeremy Bamber case. Meanwhile, I was hooked for a whole weekend on Dead Fashion Girl by Fred Vermorel. Described as “a situationist detective story” it starts with the 1954 murder of a young fashion designer in Ruislip, not far from where I live, and splays outwards and downwards into London’s postwar criminal underbelly.

The Silent Appeal by Janice Hallett is published by Profile (£20). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

Barbara, Guardian reader

You wouldn’t think that an account of a ten-month long legal process would be a page-turner, but that is exactly what Emmanuel Carrère has achieved in V13, the book based on his weekly magazine columns covering the trial of the surviving perpetrators of the terror attacks in Paris on Friday (ie Vendredi) 13, 2015. He delves into the lives of the victims, the perpetrators, the lawyers, and produces an all-round picture of the human beings involved in this horrific event. It is written with compassion, empathy, and a genuine curiosity about motivation.

Light-years away (or perhaps not) is the deceptively simple tale told by Iain Crichton Smith in Consider the Lilies, a short novel about an elderly woman’s treatment at the hands of the Duke of Sutherland as he evicted tenants during the Highland Clearances – one woman, representing the fates of 150,000. A note at the front of the book tells me that I bought it on North Uist more than half-a-century ago, and now that I’m older I find it possibly even more moving than it was then.
